chapter_theme: Under the heading அறிவுடைமை, eight verses on what understanding is worth: it is the garment that all other excellence decorates, one wise man outshines a crowd of fools, the senseless cannot be set right, the wise win the wise through the wise and keep out of company that does not value them, real ability cannot be hidden, and understanding stays where wealth comes and goes with fortune.

26.reading: A man who has no excellence through understanding cannot be made excellent by anything else, since jewels of gem and gold, sandal paste, garlands and every such ornament come only after the cloth.
26.nuance: The proverb does not dismiss ornaments; it orders them. Understanding is the cloth, the thing whose lack is nakedness, and the other goods are adornments that only make sense on a clothed body. பொறியின் in line 2 is read as 'finely wrought', qualifying the gem and gold jewels.

pazhamozhi.literal: all ornaments come after the garment

story.act: no story; the proverb states the order of dressing, cloth first and jewels after

pazhamozhi.applied_to: other excellences adorn only a man who first has understanding

27.reading: Even if a thousand men without understanding gather, they do not equal one excellent man in the wide world, just as the many stars cannot give the moonlight that the moon gives as it clears the spreading dark.
27.nuance: The argument is against number: excellence is a difference of kind, so adding fools does not approach one wise man. The quotation marks open at மதியம்போல், so the simile is printed as part of the proverb.

pazhamozhi.literal: the many stars cannot shed moonlight as the moon does

story.act: no story; the proverb sets the single moon against the crowd of stars

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one man of understanding outweighs any number of the senseless

28.reading: Those who lack good sense cannot be set firm in anything, unlike a drum that is brought to its beat by a spoken cue, lord of the good land where shining falls drop over the rock slopes, as the saying is, 'where learned knowledge has not gone in'.
28.nuance: The sense is hard to fix. Line 2 is taken as the drummer who strikes the துடி to word-signals, the responsive instrument against which the senseless are measured; the proverb's கடை is taken as the conditional 'when ... has not', so that instruction fails where learning has not first entered. Other divisions of line 2 are possible.

pazhamozhi.literal: when learned knowledge has not gone in

story.act: no story; the proverb names the condition under which a person cannot be steadied

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the senseless cannot be set right where no learning has entered

29.reading: For men of firm understanding, winning over those whose understanding matches their own worth is, lady with a deer's eyes, like the valiant great kings' binding an elephant by means of an elephant.
29.nuance: The proverb pictures the capture of a wild elephant with a trained one: the wise are drawn in only by someone of their own kind. ஆணம் in line 1 is taken as firmness or support; it can also mean affection, which would make the bond warmer. The address to a woman is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like binding an elephant with an elephant

story.act: kings capture a wild elephant by using a tame one

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the wise are won over only through those of equal understanding

30.reading: Those who have taken stock and understood alongside the discerning do not push in among people who have no regard for them, for they surely know others' natures, lord of the shore of loud waves, just as the jackal does not show itself to the reapers.
30.nuance: The understanding in question is social: knowing who will not value one and keeping away. The jackal is not cowardly in the image but shrewd; it knows the reapers with their sickles will strike. பரியார் is read as 'those without regard'.

pazhamozhi.literal: jackals do not show themselves to the reapers

story.act: no story; the jackal in the harvest field keeps out of the reapers' sight

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the discerning keep out of company that does not value them

31.reading: Need anyone put into words, for those who have themselves arranged both the fitting and the unfitting, what these are, lady of wide red-streaked eyes beneath bow brows, since he who manages much is the one who knows much?
31.nuance: Read here as a rhetorical question: one who has handled both good and bad affairs already knows them and needs no instruction. புனைந்திருந்தார் could also mean 'those adorned with' fair and foul qualities, which would turn the verse toward a person whose character speaks for itself; the proverb fits the first reading better.

pazhamozhi.literal: the one who handles much knows much

story.act: no story; the proverb credits knowledge to the one with wide charge of affairs

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the experienced need no telling what is fit and unfit

32.reading: Can men of widespread strength be hidden by covering them with moss, lady with bamboo-smooth shoulders and spear-like eyes, when no one can hide with his hand the sun that moves in the sky?
32.nuance: The verse is about திறல், ability or power, rather than understanding as such; it fits its heading only if the editor took ability as the outward show of understanding. The moss is a thin cover, as the hand is against the sun: the attempt to suppress is mocked as much as the greatness is praised.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who can hide with the hand the sun moving through the sky

story.act: no story; the proverb mocks a hand raised to cover the sun

pazhamozhi.applied_to: real ability cannot be concealed by those who would suppress it

33.reading: Fine jewels beyond price and plentiful wealth come back even after they have strayed, if their owners have fortune, lord of the great hills, but since understanding never parts from one at all, firmness, as the saying goes, gains more than fortune.
33.nuance: The verse concedes more than most praise of learning does: lost riches really can return. Its point is that their return depends on fortune, while understanding needs no return because it never leaves. The subject of பிரிவின்று is unstated and is supplied from the heading as understanding; திட்பம் is taken as the steadiness of that possession.

story.act: no story; the proverb ranks steadiness above luck

pazhamozhi.applied_to: understanding, which never leaves, is worth more than wealth that returns only by fortune

links.note: Naladiyar 131 says the beauty of hair, garment border and saffron is not beauty and only learning's is; Pazhamozhi 26 keeps the ornaments but makes understanding the garment they must follow.
links.teaches: The quatrain discards outward adornment, while the Pazhamozhi verse keeps it and ranks it, so outer graces are not worthless but parasitic on the inner one.
links.list_adds: its string of jewels, sandal and garlands is not dismissed but placed in an order, ornaments after the cloth, which the quatrain's flat denial lacks.

links.note: Kural 846 calls it folly to cover one's nakedness while leaving faults uncovered; Pazhamozhi 26 makes understanding the cloth without which ornaments are absurd.
links.teaches: Both use clothing to name what must be covered first, and together they make the senseless man's lack a nakedness that neither dress nor jewellery can hide.
links.list_adds: it sets gems, gold, sandal and garlands on the naked body, turning the couplet's single garment into a whole toilette that is wasted without understanding.

links.note: Kural 410 sets the learned against others as men against beasts; Pazhamozhi 27 says a thousand of the senseless together do not equal one excellent man.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the gap one of kind; the Pazhamozhi verse draws the consequence that numbers cannot close it, so a crowd of fools adds up to nothing.
links.list_adds: its moon and many stars turn the couplet's two-term comparison into one against a multitude, adding the argument from number.

links.note: Kural 848 describes the man who neither does what he is told nor sees for himself; Pazhamozhi 28 says the senseless cannot be set firm and gives as the condition that learning has not gone in. The link rests on an uncertain reading of 28.
links.teaches: The couplet names the double failure of the unteachable, and the Pazhamozhi verse places its cause earlier, in learning that never entered, so telling fails because nothing is there to receive it.
links.list_adds: its image of the drum that answers a spoken cue supplies the responsive learner the couplet leaves out, so the fool is measured against an instrument.

links.note: Kural 678 and Pazhamozhi 29 close on the same proverb, binding an elephant with an elephant; the Kural applies it to using one task to achieve another, Pazhamozhi to winning a wise man through a wise man.
links.teaches: The pair shows one proverb serving two ethics: in the Kural a rule of method for tasks, in Pazhamozhi a rule of persons, that only an equal can draw in an equal.
links.list_adds: it moves the elephant image from the ordering of tasks to the gaining of people, and names the kings who practise the capture.

links.note: Kural 720 says speaking before those not of one's own kind is nectar spilt in a dirty yard; Pazhamozhi 30 says the discerning do not even enter among those who have no regard for them.
links.teaches: The couplet counts the waste after one has spoken in the wrong company; the Pazhamozhi verse moves the judgement earlier, to not going in at all, and makes that avoidance itself a mark of understanding.
links.list_adds: its jackal that keeps out of the reapers' sight turns the couplet's rule of speech into a rule of where to be seen, with the danger as well as the waste.

links.note: Both use the jackal as the creature that reads its ground: in Kural 500 it kills the elephant stuck in mud, in Pazhamozhi 30 it keeps out of the reapers' sight.
links.teaches: Held together, the jackal's cunning has two faces, striking where the ground favours it and vanishing where it does not, and the Pazhamozhi verse gives the second to the wise.
links.list_adds: it turns the Kural's lesson of place in war into a lesson of social company, applied to the discerning person rather than the commander.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 32 says those of wide strength cannot be hidden, as no hand hides the sun; Naladiyar 105 shows the palm-tall great shrinking to millet size and hiding their brightness through former deeds.
links.teaches: The pair limits the proverb's confidence: no man can cover real greatness, but the Naladiyar shows it dwindling from within through old deeds, so it is safe from suppression, not from fate.
links.list_adds: its moss and raised hand make concealment a deliberate act by others, which separates it from the self-hiding the quatrain attributes to deeds.

links.note: Kural 400 calls learning the imperishable wealth and says other things are not wealth; Pazhamozhi 33 grants that jewels and riches do return to the fortunate, and ranks understanding above them because it never leaves.
links.teaches: Where the Kural denies other goods the name of wealth, the Pazhamozhi verse concedes their worth and their power to come back, and rests understanding's superiority on its independence from fortune.
links.list_adds: it names the rival goods, priceless jewels and wealth, and gives them a real but conditional permanence, so the ranking is argued rather than asserted.

links.note: Both set understanding against ornaments: in 26 ornaments come after the cloth of understanding, in 33 priceless jewels come and go with fortune while understanding stays.
links.teaches: Read together the chapter makes jewels doubly inferior to understanding, dependent on it for their sense and on fortune for their keeping.
links.list_adds: 33 adds time to 26's order of dressing, so the ornament is not only secondary but unstable.

links.note: Both prove excellence by a light in the sky: in 27 the moon that the many stars cannot equal, in 32 the sun that no hand can cover.
links.teaches: The two sky proverbs give the excellent man two properties at once, that a crowd cannot outshine him and a hand cannot put him out.
links.list_adds: 32 turns 27's contest of brightness into one of concealment, so the image moves from comparison to suppression.

source_issues: 27 lines 3-4: the quotation opens at மதியம்போல், taking the moon simile into the proverb; the proverb proper may be only பன்மீனும் காய்கலா வாகும் நிலா.
28 line 2: சொற்குறி கொண்டு துடிபண் உறுத்துவபோல் is obscure and its relation to line 1 uncertain.
31 lines 3-4: the quotation opens at அறியும் in the middle of line 3; the split அறியும் / பெரிதாள் பவனே may be a copying division.
